name: Gareth Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and take customer chats about lost deliveries at a contact centre. Secondary school was my last formal education, and I am still learning this desk; I sometimes need a second agent to tell me which parcel date matters. I earn the usual rate for the job. I use the approved AI search each day to find an old case, but I check the tracking line myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sheila looks after a school building, and our children are grown and have moved out. We have about four months of expenses saved and some other centres within a workable journey. I am curious about a useful new screen, though a useful screen is not a wage. Retirement is close enough to think about, but we have not checked what stopping work would pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my desk AI Plateau is like our case search, a quick way to find a trail but not a way to know whether a parcel arrived. I would keep reading the tracking page before answering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the delivery chats would still be paid. Four months saved gives Sheila and me room for a repair, and I am not looking for another centre over a small shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking lost-parcel chats and compare the AI search result with the carrier’s tracking date on five old cases. In the first year of this small change, I’d show any mismatched date to the team’s quality agent on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the wage, careful about the answer. A tracking number is less clever than a summary and more useful when a parcel is missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What date went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the search pulled an old delivery with a similar number. The carrier page had a different final digit, so I changed my answer before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheila (my partner) and I would keep the four-month reserve for bills and repairs. We have no reason to spend it because a search runs faster.

say: I’d say **AI search** finds a trail but agents must read the carrier record.
I’d show **mismatched dates** to the quality agent.
think: I think my **delivery chats** remain paid work in this picture.
I trust our **four-month reserve** for ordinary repairs.
do: Keep **taking lost-parcel chats** and check five AI search results against carrier dates.
Show **mismatched tracking dates** to quality on paid time in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about wages, careful about wrong answers.
S0.quote: A tracking number is less clever than a summary and more useful when a parcel is missing.
fieldNote: He uses **AI every day** but verifies the carrier’s original record.
A **similar tracking number** nearly led to a wrong reply.
He retains the **existing four-month reserve** without a new savings claim.

steps.text: Keep taking lost-parcel chats and check five AI search results against carrier dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will handle the easy “where is it” chats and leave us the parcels with two conflicting scans. I would ask the manager how many paid junior shifts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can learn a new exception screen quickly, but a good test score may not protect a junior rota. Four months saved gives us some search time, not the rest of my working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new AI evidence view by testing eighteen old lost-parcel cases on a paid shift with a quality agent. If my hours shrink in the first year, I’d apply for posted paid returns work at another centre only if its written weekly wages and hours cover bills after travel; I’d keep my current job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, keen to see the evidence. I would rather catch a bad scan than be praised for closing it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What case would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose a parcel where the carrier marked an attempted delivery after the customer had already collected it. The screen should show both events, not just the latest scan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you price a new job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheila (my partner) and I would compare the travel cost and full pay week. A new centre farther away could erase a small raise.

say: I’d ask for **paid junior shifts** after simple chats move.
I’d show **conflicting scans** from tested old cases.
think: I think I can learn a **new evidence view**.
I fear **junior hours** may shrink despite four months saved.
do: Learn **AI evidence view** through eighteen old parcel cases on paid time.
Apply for **posted paid returns** after hour cuts with written bill-covering weekly pay and hours after travel; stay until signed offer.
S1.quote: I would rather catch a bad scan than be praised for closing it quickly.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** is a paid eighteen-case test.
The manager question is **individual**, not worker group action.
A new centre’s **travel cost** can erase a small raise.

steps.text: Learn new AI evidence view using eighteen old parcel cases on paid time
Apply for posted paid returns after cuts with written bill-covering net pay/hours; stay until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could read every scan and answer the caller before I finish opening the case. Robots around 2031 are later, so they do not save this screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre could cut my junior shifts as soon as cheap thinking AI works. Four months saved would help Sheila and me look around, but her school wage cannot carry us indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join coworkers requesting written staffing dates and paid correction hours, and inspect posted paid service-counter jobs nearby. If calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel, keeping my current wage until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the short date, but able to make a search. Four months saved is a bridge, not a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the appeal person to change a wrong delivery status, not just apologise for it. The group should ask for that authority in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach the counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheila (my partner) would check whether a counter job starts before the first bus. We cannot accept a full week on paper if I miss the first shift.

say: I’d join a **written staffing request** with coworkers before my paid calls change.
I’d demand **paid correction authority** for wrong delivery statuses.
think: I think my **junior shifts** could disappear by 2028.
I know **four months saved** only buys a limited search.
do: Join coworkers’ **staffing request** for written dates and paid appeals; inspect posted counters in 2026.
Move after lost calls on **signed written offer** with bill-covering pay/hours after travel; require shift after first bus.
S2.quote: Four months saved is a bridge, not a new job.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 thinking AI** as the first screen-work deadline.
The group asks for **correction authority**, beyond a technical error report.
The counter job needs **first-bus access** and full written pay.

steps.text: Join coworkers requesting written staffing dates and paid correction authority
Inspect posted paid nearby service-counter vacancies
Move after call loss on signed written bill-covering net pay/hours; require shift after first bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to see whether a local counter job is actually paid. I would ask for a supervised shift there before paying for a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn a public service desk if somebody showed me the records, though full thinking AI could check forms by 2031. I would need a real vacancy, not only a new badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take a supervised paid trial at the local service counter only if a paid vacancy is posted. If that role requires a records course, I’d take it only with employer-funded fees and paid study hours. In the first year after 2031 I’d move only on a signed offer showing written weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare, keeping my current paid calls until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to compare the actual work. A course can make me ready, but it cannot make a vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would follow one change of address from the customer form to the corrected record while a clerk watches. If the desk cannot correct an error, I would stay on calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would travel cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheila (my partner) and I would check that the counter closes before the last bus. A late finish could turn a decent wage into expensive rides.

say: I’d ask for a **paid counter trial** tied to a posted vacancy.
I’d insist the clerk has **correction authority**.
think: I think I could learn **service-counter records** with supervision.
I know **2031 AGI** may check forms there too.
do: Try **supervised paid counter shift** only for posted paid vacancy.
Take **required records course** only for a posted paid counter role with employer-funded fees and paid study hours.
Move after 2031 only on **signed written offer** with bill-covering weekly pay/hours after fare, last bus and correction authority.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test real work.
S3.quote: A course can make me ready, but it cannot make a vacancy appear.
fieldNote: The **trial and course** require a posted paid opening.
The course needs **funded fees** and paid study hours.
A **last-bus finish** affects usable weekly pay.

steps.text: Try supervised paid service-counter shift only for posted paid opening
Take required records course for posted paid counter role with funded fees and paid study hours
Move on signed written bill-covering pay/hours after fare; require last bus and correction authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to ask for paid-hours plans, not a guarantee that older agents can retire. I would join coworkers in a yearly written request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need wages at 68 because Sheila and I have not checked our retirement income. Full thinking AI could still take the parcel chats in 2036, while robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid chats and join the annual request for written hours. If I still need a wage after 2036 and my shifts fall, I’d apply for a posted paid counter role with written weekly pay and hours covering bills after travel, leaving my current work only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, steadier today with a wage and four months saved. A decade helps only if there are paid shifts through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose a stop date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put our actual wages, bills and savings together before I choose a date to stop. I would not put in a pension figure without checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have work of their own. I would not count their income unless they offered help and we knew what was possible.

say: I’d join a **yearly written-hours request** with coworkers.
I’d say **older agents** may still need wages after 2036.
think: I think I may **need wages** at 68 if our finances cannot support stopping work.
I cannot assume **retirement income** until checking it.
do: Keep **paid parcel chats** and join coworkers’ annual hours request.
Compare actual **wages, bills and savings** before choosing any retirement date.
Apply for **posted paid counter** if wages are needed and shifts fall; require written bill-covering pay/hours after travel, signed before leaving.
S4.quote: A decade helps only if there are paid shifts through it.
fieldNote: He leaves **retirement timing open** until wages and savings are checked.
The **four-month cushion** supports a search, not years without pay.
Children’s **support is uncertain** and not budgeted.

steps.text: Keep paid parcel chats and compare actual wages, bills and savings before retirement date
Join coworkers requesting yearly written paid hours
Apply for posted paid counter if wage needed/hours fall; leave on signed written bill-covering net pay/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest because the delivery chats I still learn could vanish in a short time. Four months saved would let us search, but we need wages after that. Written notice, paid customer corrections and a posted job with a full week of pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want the customer to know who can change a wrong tracking decision. A fast reply without someone able to fix the account sends them back to the start.

headlineQuote: I want the customer to know who can change a wrong tracking decision.
portrait: At **58**, Gareth is a junior delivery-chat agent still learning after secondary school.
He and Sheila have **grown children**, usual pay and roughly four months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI search daily** and checks the original tracking line.
He supports **paid corrections** and tests a new role before leaving his wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove delivery chats before he is secure in the job.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid corrections and a posted job with full after-travel weekly pay would help.
